title: 09. Production & Safety: Day 4 — Dependencies and Testing
summary: So far your agents have been stateless: same prompt, same model, same behavior. Real agents need context — who the user is, what database to talk to, which API token to use.
objectives: Why Dependency Injection Matters for Agents

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: So far your agents have been stateless: same prompt, same model, same behavior. Real agents need **context** — who the user is, what database to talk to, which API token to use. Pydantic AI handles this with a **`Deps` container** that you pass at runtime. Today you will inject dependencies, type them properly, and then unit-test your agents using **`TestModel`** and **`FunctionModel`** without ever calling a real LLM.

sections.title: Why Dependency Injection Matters for Agents
sections.body:
Three forces push you toward DI:

1. **Testing** — you do not want every `pytest` run to burn OpenAI credits and flake on rate limits. You want to swap the model and any external clients for fakes.
2. **Multi-tenancy** — the same agent code must serve Ada, Bob, and Carla with their own settings, mailboxes, and permissions. Baking user IDs into the system prompt is brittle.
3. **Environment separation** — dev uses a sandboxed DB, prod uses the real one. Same agent, different `Deps`.

Pydantic AI's answer: declare a `deps_type` on the agent, pass `deps=` when you call `run()`, and read `ctx.deps` inside tools. The type system guarantees tools cannot access fields that don't exist.

sections.title: Defining a Deps Container
sections.body:
Use a `@dataclass` for plain data, or a Pydantic `BaseModel` when you want validation. Dataclasses are the common choice — fast, no overhead, and `mypy`/`pyright` understand them perfectly.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

@dataclass
class EmailDeps:
    user_name: str
    user_tone: Literal["formal", "casual", "concise"]
    signature: str
    max_body_chars: int = 2000  # sensible default
```

The agent is generic over this type:

```python
from pydantic_ai import Agent, RunContext

email_agent = Agent(
    "openai:gpt-4o-mini",
    deps_type=EmailDeps,
    system_prompt="You draft emails on behalf of the user. Always use the draft_email tool.",
)
```

`Agent[Deps, Result]` is the underlying generic — `email_agent` is now `Agent[EmailDeps, str]`. `mypy` will complain if a tool tries to read `ctx.deps.tenant_id` because that field does not exist on `EmailDeps`.

sections.title: RunContext[Deps] in Tools
sections.body:
Tools that need context take `ctx: RunContext[YourDeps]` as the first argument. Tools that don't need context use `@agent.tool_plain` instead (Day 3).

```python
@email_agent.tool
def draft_email(ctx: RunContext[EmailDeps], subject: str, body: str) -> str:
    """Draft a complete email, applying the user's tone and signature."""
    # ctx.deps is typed as EmailDeps — IDE autocomplete works
    if len(body) > ctx.deps.max_body_chars:
        body = body[: ctx.deps.max_body_chars] + "…"
    return f"Subject: {subject}\n\n{body}\n\n— {ctx.deps.user_name}\n{ctx.deps.signature}"
```

Two things to notice. First, `ctx.deps` is fully typed — your editor will autocomplete `user_name`, `user_tone`, etc. Second, the tool can use deps to enforce policy (here, truncating long bodies), not just to format strings.

sections.title: Passing Deps at Runtime
sections.body:
`deps=` is a runtime argument to `run()`. The same agent instance can be reused with different deps across calls — no need to rebuild the agent per user.

```python
import asyncio

async def main() -> None:
    deps = EmailDeps(
        user_name="Ada Lovelace",
        user_tone="formal",
        signature="Founder, Analytical Engines Inc.",
    )
    result = await email_agent.run(
        "Draft an email to Charles asking if we can meet next Tuesday at 2pm.",
        deps=deps,
    )
    print(result.data)

asyncio.run(main())
```

Forget `deps=` and `ctx.deps` will be `None` at runtime — see Common Pitfalls.

sections.title: Example 1: Full User-Aware Email Drafter
sections.body:
Putting it together, here is the complete file you can save as `email_drafter.py` and run:

```python
# email_drafter.py
import asyncio
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

from pydantic_ai import Agent, RunContext

@dataclass
class EmailDeps:
    user_name: str
    user_tone: Literal["formal", "casual", "concise"]
    signature: str
    max_body_chars: int = 2000

email_agent = Agent(
    "openai:gpt-4o-mini",
    deps_type=EmailDeps,
    system_prompt=(
        "You draft emails on the user's behalf. "
        "Always call draft_email with subject and body. "
        "Match the user's tone from context."
    ),
)

@email_agent.tool
def draft_email(ctx: RunContext[EmailDeps], subject: str, body: str) -> str:
    """Compose a final email using the user's signature and tone."""
    tone_hint = {
        "formal": "Dear",
        "casual": "Hey",
        "concise": "",
    }[ctx.deps.user_tone]
    if tone_hint:
        body = f"{tone_hint} —\n\n{body}"
    if len(body) > ctx.deps.max_body_chars:
        body = body[: ctx.deps.max_body_chars] + "…"
    return f"Subject: {subject}\n\n{body}\n\n— {ctx.deps.user_name}\n{ctx.deps.signature}"

@email_agent.system_prompt
def add_tone_instruction(ctx: RunContext[EmailDeps]) -> str:
    return f"The user's preferred tone is {ctx.deps.user_tone}."

async def main() -> None:
    deps = EmailDeps(
        user_name="Ada Lovelace",
        user_tone="formal",
        signature="Founder, Analytical Engines Inc.",
    )
    result = await email_agent.run(
        "Draft an email to Charles asking for a Tuesday 2pm meeting.",
        deps=deps,
    )
    print(result.data)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

Notice `@email_agent.system_prompt` — it lets you inject dynamic, deps-aware instructions into the system prompt. The function runs every `run()` call.

sections.title: Example 2: Multi-Tenant Task Agent
sections.body:
Now a more realistic case: same agent code, different users backed by different database rows. Use a `Protocol` so production can swap the real DB for a fake in tests.

```python
# task_agent.py
import asyncio
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Protocol

from pydantic_ai import Agent, RunContext

class Database(Protocol):
    async def get_tasks(self, user_id: str) -> list[str]: ...
    async def add_task(self, user_id: str, task: str) -> None: ...

@dataclass
class TaskDeps:
    user_id: str
    db: Database

task_agent = Agent(
    "openai:gpt-4o-mini",
    deps_type=TaskDeps,
    system_prompt="You manage the user's task list. Be terse.",
)

@task_agent.tool
async def list_my_tasks(ctx: RunContext[TaskDeps]) -> list[str]:
    """Return the current user's tasks."""
    return await ctx.deps.db.get_tasks(ctx.deps.user_id)

@task_agent.tool
async def add_task(ctx: RunContext[TaskDeps], task: str) -> str:
    """Add a task for the current user."""
    await ctx.deps.db.add_task(ctx.deps.user_id, task)
    return f"Added '{task}' for {ctx.deps.user_id}."

class FakeDB:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.store: dict[str, list[str]] = {}

    async def get_tasks(self, user_id: str) -> list[str]:
        return self.store.get(user_id, [])

    async def add_task(self, user_id: str, task: str) -> None:
        self.store.setdefault(user_id, []).append(task)

async def main() -> None:
    db = FakeDB()
    await db.add_task("ada", "Buy punch cards")

    result = await task_agent.run(
        "What's on my list? Add 'Email Charles' too.",
        deps=TaskDeps(user_id="ada", db=db),
    )
    print(result.data)
    print("DB now:", db.store)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

The agent doesn't know whether `db` is `FakeDB` or a `PostgresPool` — it only knows the `Protocol`. That is the whole point.

sections.title: Testing with TestModel
sections.body:
`TestModel` is a fake model that returns canned responses, exercises your tools, and records what it did. Import it from `pydantic_ai.models.test`:

```python
from pydantic_ai.models.test import TestModel

async def demo_test_model() -> None:
    test_model = TestModel()
    email_agent.model = test_model  # hot-swap the model

    deps = EmailDeps(user_name="T", user_tone="casual", signature="-- T")
    result = await email_agent.run("hello", deps=deps)

    print("Result:", result.data)
    print("Called tools:", test_model.called_tools)
    print("Params:", test_model.last_model_request_parameters)
```

Two properties matter:

- **`called_tools`** — list of tool names the model invoked this run. Useful for asserting "the agent called `draft_email`."
- **`last_model_request_parameters`** — the `ModelRequestParameters` Pydantic AI built, including function tool schemas. Useful for asserting tools are exposed correctly.

By default `TestModel` calls the first tool in the agent and returns whatever the tool returns. It does **not** validate that the model's tool-call args match the schema — see Common Pitfalls.

sections.title: Testing with FunctionModel
sections.body:
`FunctionModel` gives you full control: you provide a function that decides what the "model" returns. Use it to simulate edge cases — wrong tool, malformed args, multiple tool calls.

```python
from pydantic_ai.models.test import FunctionModel
from pydantic_ai.messages import ModelResponse, ToolCallPart, TextPart

def always_call_draft_email(messages, info):
    """Pretend the model always picks draft_email with fixed args."""
    return ModelResponse(parts=[
        ToolCallPart(tool_name="draft_email",
                     args={"subject": "Hi", "body": "Hello there"}),
    ])

async def demo_function_model() -> None:
    email_agent.model = FunctionModel(always_call_draft_email)
    deps = EmailDeps(user_name="T", user_tone="formal", signature="-- T")
    result = await email_agent.run("say hi", deps=deps)
    assert "Subject: Hi" in result.data
```

`FunctionModel` is invaluable for testing failure modes — e.g., a model that calls a non-existent tool, or passes a string where an int is required.

sections.title: A pytest Example: Tone-Respecting Drafter
sections.body:
Here is a real test file. Save as `test_email_drafter.py`:

```python
# test_email_drafter.py
import pytest
from pydantic_ai.models.test import TestModel, FunctionModel
from pydantic_ai.messages import ModelResponse, ToolCallPart

from email_drafter import email_agent, EmailDeps

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_formal_tone_includes_dear():
    email_agent.model = TestModel()
    deps = EmailDeps(user_name="Ada", user_tone="formal", signature="-- Ada")
    result = await email_agent.run("draft a hello", deps=deps)
    # The formal tone prepends "Dear —" to the body
    assert "Dear —" in result.data
    assert "-- Ada" in result.data

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_draft_email_tool_was_called():
    tm = TestModel()
    email_agent.model = tm
    deps = EmailDeps(user_name="Ada", user_tone="casual", signature="-- A")
    await email_agent.run("draft something", deps=deps)
    assert "draft_email" in tm.called_tools

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_bogus_tool_triggers_no_crash():
    # Simulate a model that calls a tool we don't have
    def bogus_tool(messages, info):
        return ModelResponse(parts=[
            ToolCallPart(tool_name="nonexistent_tool", args={}),
        ])
    email_agent.model = FunctionModel(bogus_tool)
    deps = EmailDeps(user_name="Ada", user_tone="casual", signature="-- A")
    result = await email_agent.run("oops", deps=deps)
    # Pydantic AI auto-retries with a correction message; final result still str
    assert isinstance(result.data, str)
```

Run with `pytest -q`. Note the third test — Pydantic AI intercepts invalid tool calls, sends a correction back to the model, and retries. `FunctionModel` lets you assert the framework's behavior under bad model output.

sections.title: Common Pitfalls
sections.body:
- **Forgetting `deps=` at runtime.** `ctx.deps` will be `None` and your tool will raise `AttributeError`. Always type `ctx.deps` so your IDE warns you.
- **Mutable deps shared across runs.** If `Deps` holds a `list` or `dict` you mutate, two concurrent `run()` calls will clobber each other. Copy or use immutable structures, or scope deps per call.
- **`TestModel` does not validate tool args.** It will happily call your tool with garbage kwargs and your test passes while production breaks. Use `FunctionModel` for schema-level assertions, and add `@field_validator` inside your tool's args if you need guarantees.
- **Reusing a single `TestModel` across tests.** `called_tools` accumulates. Create a fresh `TestModel()` per test, or call `test_model = TestModel()` in each test function.
- **Importing `TestModel` from the wrong place.** It lives in `pydantic_ai.models.test`, not `pydantic_ai`.
